L115: Figure 【64†22.4.2】 depicts the fundamental unit cell in the $z$-plane, with vertices $\text{s}=0$, $\text{c}=K$, $\text{d}=K+\mathrm{i}{K}^{\prime }$, $\text{n}=\mathrm{i}{K}^{\prime }$. The set of points $z=mK+n\mathrm{i}{K}^{\prime }$, $m,n\in \mathbb{Z}$, comprise the lattice for the 12 Jacobian functions; all other lattice unit cells are generated by translation of the fundamental unit cell by $mK+n\mathrm{i}{K}^{\prime }$, where again $m,n\in \mathbb{Z}$.
L116: Figure 22.4.2: $z$-plane. Fundamental unit cell. 【65†Magnify】

L130: Using the p,q notation of (【72†22.2.10】), Figure 【64†22.4.2】 serves as a mnemonic for the poles, zeros, periods, and half-periods of the 12 Jacobian elliptic functions as follows. Let p,q be any two distinct letters from the set s,c,d,n which appear in counterclockwise orientation at the corners of all lattice unit cells. Then: (a) In any lattice unit cell $\mathrm{p}\mathrm{q}(z,k)$ has a simple zero at $z=\text{p}$ and a simple pole at $z=\text{q}$.
L131: (b) The difference between p and the nearest q is a half-period of $\mathrm{p}\mathrm{q}(z,k)$. This half-period will be plus or minus a member of the triple $K,\mathrm{i}{K}^{\prime },K+\mathrm{i}{K}^{\prime }$; the other two members of this triple are quarter periods of $\mathrm{p}\mathrm{q}(z,k)$.
